newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Jospin seeks to shed "decent loser" tag.
newsitem.headline: France's Jospin seeks to shed "decent loser" tag.

text.p: French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin, who won the mantle of "decent loser" when he narrowly lost the presidency to Jacques Chirac in 1995, is projecting a new combativeness ahead of snap parliamentary elections in May.

Chirac's surprise decision to call polls 10 months early has forced France's biggest and most fractious opposition party to rally behind its chief, and given Jospin the leeway to impose his campaign agenda.
If the left wins, which recent opinion polls suggest is an outside possibility, he would be the natural candidate for prime minister, sharing power with the conservative president.
Whether the professorial Jospin can shake off the "decent loser" tag he won by scoring 47.3 percent against Chirac in May 1995 depends as much on his personality as his manifesto.

"Many voters are still undecided and Jospin may be the tortoise to Chirac's hare," editor Laurent Joffrin wrote in the daily Liberation on Tuesday. "The game is perfectly open... rarely has the Left seen such favourable electoral territory."

Jospin set out his campaign themes shortly after Monday night's presidential announcement in a television address. He accused the government of planning a new wave of austerity, therefore worsening unemployment, in order to qualify France for a single European currency.
Over the past few months, several political blows have bruised the popularity of the Socialist Party and its silver-haired, bespectacled leader.
It humiliatingly lost the southern town of Vitrolles to the far-right, anti-immigration National Front in a nationally watched municipal election in February.

Days later, artists and intellectuals launched protests against a government bill to clamp down on illegal immigration. An embarrassed Jospin, keen not to alienate grassroots voters exasperated by immigration, jumped on the bandwagon late.

In the past month, revelations that the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand personally supervised illegal bugging of lawyers, journalists and politicians have tarnished his heirs, although Jospin has tried to distance today's Socialist Party from this burdensome legacy.

The popular Guignols de l'Info (news clowns) television show has long lampooned Jospin as "Yoyo", a bumbling simpleton based on Enid Blyton's children's classic Noddy, driving a toy car in search of ideas. His lieutenants are depicted tearing their hair out at his feebleness.

The price of his lack of charisma and combativity has been a slight revival of the ruling centre-right coalition in opinion polls after a period when the Socialists and their left-wing allies had edged within striking distance.
Jospin sounded more vigorous when he set his campaign tone just after Chirac's announcement, saying the government was preparing "a new step towards a harsh capitalism".
Chirac was seeking to pre-empt the failure of his economic policies, prepare tougher austerity and head off sleaze scandals threatening members of his coalition, Jospin charged.

With only 63 out of 577 seats after a 1993 landslide defeat, the Socialists need support from leftist allies if they are to win. Jospin has successfully forged electoral pacts with the Greens and with the small Radical Socialist party.
He is now trying to woo the Communists, a much tougher prospect, by refusing to introduce further austerity measures to ensure France meets the strict targets for a single European currency.
The son of a schoolteacher, Jospin attended the elite National Administrative College (ENA) and joined the Foreign Ministry, before dropping out to become an economics lecturer.
He describes himself as "warm, straightforward and simple" in private, and says he knows how to have fun but concedes: "A sense of modesty cramps and confines me a little."

After the media focused on his strict Protestant upbringing in an overwhelmingly Catholic country, Jospin countered by telling an interviewer how he had turned a boyhood dream into reality by buying a sporty convertible car.
